However, while Zebra Sharks are fecund, a large percentage of yolked eggs degrade or spoil within the first few weeks post-oviposition. Therefore, ultrasonography represents a potential tool that could be used to both accurately distinguish fertile from non-fertile eggs and to diagnose changes in early embryonic development predictive of poor outcomes. Freshly laid eggs from four female Zebra Sharks were collected by aquarists daily from two enclosures at Aquarium of the Pacific. Eggs were incubated undisturbed for two or three weeks at 23.8 – 25˚C and then underwent weekly exams via ultrasound to monitor embryo development. Eggs were evaluated for: yolk integrity, egg case fluid homogeneity and embryo morphology. Abnormalities were observed in the majority of samples (n = 69, 67%) as early as 16 days to 93 days post-oviposition. Common abnormalities included: bent or curled tails, anechoic fluid pockets forming at the attachment of the yolk stalk to the yolk, and sluggish movement. Ultrasonography was found to be an effective and non-invasive method to determine egg fertility, identify embryos with developmental abnormalities and track growth rates.
4273: The freshwater (or largetooth) sawfish (Pristis pristis) is a benthic, diadromous ray whose geographic range was the largest of all sawfishes, spanning across the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic Oceans. However, their abundance has declined >60% due to overfishing and habitat loss. Now this species is rare across most of its former range except in Australia, and is currently listed as Critically Endangered on the IUCN’s Red List of Threatened and Endangered Species. The Fitzroy River in the Kimberly region of north-western Australia is an important nursery habitat for P. pristis, and is relatively pristine due to its remoteness, lack of coastal development, low human population density, and low commercial fishing pressure. The Fitzroy River is a large (~100,000 km2), highly dynamic system with distinct wet and dry seasons and occasional flooding that is known to influence P. pristis recruitment into the river. The river is now being considered for water resource development, but previous genetic studies have given contradictory results on dispersal and population structuring, making it difficult to formulate a conservation plan. This study will analyze ~300 DNA samples collected from P. pristis in the Fitzroy River over the past two decades to determine kinship, relatedness, and recruitment patterns using thousands of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) generated with next-generation sequencing technology. With these findings, we can provide a better understanding of P. pristis reproductive ecology to assess and manage threats affecting mortality rates within critical reproductive habitats, paving the way for more effective conservation of this at-risk predator.
4274: Marine pollution is an ongoing problem that affects many fish and wildlife species, including the endangered smalltooth sawfish, Pristis pectinata. On 8 February 2023, a badly entangled 15-foot-long adult female was found by anglers in the Ten Thousand Islands, Florida, which was reported to the U.S. Sawfish Recovery Hotline. At that time, the fish was still strong and eluded the anglers. However, when it was reported again on 15 March 2023, the entanglement had become worse, and the fish had become lethargic. A charter captain and state law enforcement staff monitored the fish while permitted research staff mobilized. We discovered that a stone crab trap float line was deeply embedded around the rostrum and wrapped around the emaciated body, with the 40-pound trap still attached, dragging behind. After removing all debris, the fish was tagged with an acoustic transmitter and safely released. Consensus with the team was that this fish was close to death. Two months later, we detected this fish near the mouth of the Caloosahatchee River, Florida, about 80 km north, indicating it survived the ordeal and was recovering. The U.S. Sawfish Recovery Hotline is a key tool that promotes recovery of this species, including successful responses to injured individuals.
4275: Despite their importance to organismal and ecosystem success, symbiotic associations in marine environments are often poorly understood. This is particularly true for interactions involving highly mobile or migratory species where it is difficult to observe symbioses over time. In the case of manta rays, casual and temporary associations with fish and other hitchhiker species is documented, but the extent of these interactions and the stability of symbiotic relationships over time remains relatively unknown. Here we assessed eight years of manta (M. cf. birostris) visual survey data to categorize the stability of individual manta-associated fish aggregates over time and identify the relative spatial variance of those associations on the manta ray. Surveys were conducted by free divers from small vessels in south Florida and included extensive video collection. Videos were analyzed for individual manta identification and symbiont species identification, count, and spatial position relative to the host. Preliminary results indicate variation in individual manta community structure over time but relative spatial consistency across symbiotic species. Studying manta-associated fish aggregates and symbiont community structure may help us understand the ecological importance of these associations and their potential to serve as markers of stability in ecological communities. In order to adequately conserve and protect these charismatic rays, it is critically important to understand how they interact with and support the ecosystems they exist in.
4276: Indo-Pacific Lionfish (Pterois volitans) are a well-established invasive species in the western Atlantic that have been observed on deep reefs down to ~300m. Lionfish presence on deep reefs is concerning given their negative impacts on biodiversity and recruitment seen on shallow reefs. Deep reef fish communities are poorly known, but preliminary studies indicate that deep reefs are home to many rare, undescribed, or highly endemic species, making them highly vulnerable to lionfish predation. Understanding what lionfish are eating and how they are moving on the reef is a necessary first step to understand what impact these foreign predators will have on rariphotic communities in the Atlantic. Using spearfishing and a manned submersible, 137 lionfish were collected off the southern coast of Curacao down to 200m. Gut contents were identified using a combination of visual identification and DNA metabarcoding of the mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase I gene. DNA sequences were matched to a custom database of 16,000+ sequences from fishes collected in the Western Atlantic. Lionfish collected across the reef slope are feeding on deep- and shallow-reef prey species. N=51 different species were detected, far more than using visual techniques alone. Commonly detected genera include Chromis, Corphopterus, Apogon, and Stegastes. Our results provide key insight as to the threats lionfish may pose to vulnerable deep-reef ecosystems.
4277: Fisheries biology of elasmobranchs has undergone scrutiny over the course of several decades, yet our knowledge of the time-spatial movement of these animals remains limited. Particularly noteworthy is the proclivity of endangered elasmobranchs to engage in expansive migratory patterns spanning diverse aquatic domains. Consequently, the imperative for international collaboration is underscored, as such cooperative endeavors are integral to the effective implementation of sustainable management strategies for elasmobranch populations. In recent years, acoustic telemetry has become a convenient tool for tracking research and is gradually being widely utilized. Properly setting up receiver arrays, choosing suitable tags, and adopting effective tagging methods are conducive to advancing research. This project progressively deployed receivers in the surrounding waters of Taiwan and collaborated with other acoustical telemetry teams since 2023. Currently, we have set up 14 receivers in both the eastern and western waters of Taiwan, including Yilan, Hualien, Taitung, Dongsha, and Penghu. Simultaneously, this research placed transmitters on/in 26 cartilaginous fish and released them, including external transmitters on 12 whale sharks (Rhincodon typus), 4 Taiwanese wedgefish (Rhynchobatus immaculatus), 3 brown guitarfish (Rhinobatos schlegelii), and 1 white-spotted bambooshark (Chiloscyllium plagiosum), as well as internal transmitters through surgery in 5 sicklefin lemon sharks (Negaprion acutidens) and 1 tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier). In forthcoming work, we plan to set up more receivers, tag and release various endangered elasmobranchs, and actively seek collaborations in acoustic telemetry. This project aims to provide more favorable references for the sustainable management of elasmobranch resources in the future.
4278: Schooling in fishes increases foraging success and decreases predation risk, and sensory input from the lateral line system (LL) plays an important role. Previous studies have examined the effects of ocean acidification (OA, elevated CO2) on other larval fish behaviors, here we present the first results on the effects of OA on schooling and development of the LL in silversides from fertilization to 25 days post hatch (dph) under control (400 µatm, ~8.15 pH) and elevated (4200 µatm, ~7.20 pH) pCO2 conditions. Onset of schooling was inferred from changes in the distance distribution between larvae (from 2 to 25 dph) obtained from thousands of calibrated digital images. We found evidence that CO2 delays the onset of schooling by 10 dph (control at 8 vs. elevated at 18 dph), as marked by a change in distance distributions (from random to a ,clumped’, ‘schooling’ pattern). This might be due to differences in timing of neuromast differentiation and LL canal development, which we subsequently assessed with fluorescent staining (4-di-2-ASP) and SEM, respectively. Preliminary analyses show no differences in the timing of increase in neuromast numbers or in the timing of LL canal development between CO2 treatments. Further work is needed to explain this result, as a delay in the onset of schooling is predicted to be detrimental to larval foraging and ultimately to survival.
4279: Across animal taxa, visual acuity is positively correlated with eye size. Several factors have certainly influenced the evolution of larger eyes and, hence, of superior visual capacity. In aquatic organisms, water turbidity and light intensity are well known selective factors of eye size. However, the social environment can also exert strong selective pressures on visual capacity and, in particular, the type of female sexual selection might represent an additional factor that shapes the evolution of eye size. In this study, we focused on viviparous fishes of the family Poeciliidae to compare optimal eye size between species in which females rely on the visual evaluation of males (pre-copulatory sexual selection) and species in which females do not visually examine their potential mates but instead apparently rely on cryptic female choice (post-copulatory sexual selection). Using modern phylogenetic comparative methods, we found that species that exhibit pre-copulatory female choice have slightly larger eyes compared to species that exhibit post-copulatory female choice. In addition, we analyzed the influence of different proxies for water turbidity and predation pressure, which are environmental factors that could have also contributed to the evolution of eye size. However, we found no effects of these proxies on the variation among species in eye size. Our findings suggest that the visual evaluation of males by females that occurs in some species has contributed to the evolution of larger eyes and presumably enhanced visual acuity compared to species in which females rely to a greater extent on cryptic female choice.
4280: Ocean acidification is known to affect numerous traits in early life history stages of fishes, but the experimental results do not allow generalizations to be made. It has been suggested that species resilient to elevated CO2 levels inhabit more CO2-variable inshore environments, but what about species that move between inshore and offshore bottom habitats? We determined the CO2-sensitivity of the larvae of northern stock Black Sea Bass (Centropristis striata, BSB), an ecologically and economically important fish that migrates from offshore overwintering grounds to coastal spawning and nursery areas. We reared larvae from wild-caught fish at three pCO2 levels (~400, ~2200, ~3000 µatm), from 0 to 10 days post hatch (dph, onset of flexion and end of the initial exogenous feeding stage). No statistical effects of pCO2 were found on hatching success or survival to 10 dph. Larval growth increased with increasing pCO2 (0.11→0.17 mm d-1), with ‘extreme’ individuals growing 55% faster (were 1.2× larger) than control conditions (~400 µatm). BSB larvae may thus acquire their surprisingly high CO2 tolerance either via high CO2 exposure in inshore spawning grounds or via parental exposure to high CO2 in productive inshore environments or at offshore depths during overwintering.

4284: Sultanate of Oman is well known for the high fish species biodiversity with more than 1000 species documented in its territorial seawater. This is mainly attributed to the large diversity of marine ecosystems along its coastline of more than 3600 km, and distributed within Arabian Sea, Sea of Oman and Arabian Gulf. Among the Omani fish groups that has received a limited research and independent surveys is the elasmobranchs (sharks and rays). In Oman, elasmobranchs are landed as both targeted and by-catch with more than 95% of the production derived from artisanal fishing activities. However, information on fisheries and diversity of elasmobranchs in Oman is scarce. Being Oman is ranked second in marine fisheries production in MENA regions, make it a must-study region for elasmobranchs fishery and diversity. The present study was undertaken as a focused study on batoids diversity and fisheries in the Sultanate of Oman with several species of rays were identified as new records. The diagnostic features of these species are presented along with their photographs.

4285: Chondrichthyans integral to oceanic biodiversity for over 400 million years face significant threats, primarily driven by human activities. Scientific research, vital for their conservation and understanding of vertebrate evolution, raises ethical concerns due to potential harm at individual and population levels. Capture, handling, and implantation of tracking devices though essential for research, prompt ethical considerations. Ensuring Chondrichthyan's welfare and adhering to ethical considerations demands an integral approach. Key considerations include implementing adequate capture methods, reducing handling time, and using sedation during research to minimise stress and trauma. As well as considering post-traumatic stress (usually not visible by the researchers). Rehabilitation and rehoming/rewilding efforts must balance with the recognition of animals returning to natural habitats, prioritising the release of those capable of survival in the wild and avoiding unnecessary long-term captivity. Importantly, indigenous perspectives, deeply rooted in the ocean and its wildlife, are vital. This paper explores the ethical challenges in Chondrichthyan's research, emphasising the need for transparency and responsible technology use. As Australian institutions are moving towards aligning with the Openness Agreement on Animal Research and Teaching, balancing scientific progress while truly considering and respecting the intrinsic value of individual animals is imperative.

4286: The giant shovelnose ray (GSR) (Glaucostegus typus) is found in coastal waters spanning 18 countries. Juveniles primarily inhabit intertidal areas where benthic invertebrate-rich substrate provides ample feeding opportunities. Without predation pressures from large-bodied predators, these sites serve as fantastic nursery grounds for young rays. Regardless of their Critically Endangered IUCN status, our understanding of their feeding ecology and resource utilization in these intertidal habitats remains limited. Learning about how juvenile GSRs obtain resources is valuable for understanding how they interact with trophic food webs and the local environment. This research examines the feeding ecology of juvenile GSRs at Lucinda Beach, where this species is highly abundant. Gastric lavage, a non-lethal method for obtaining stomach contents, was trialed on juvenile GSRs to detail their prey consumption and assess foraging strategy within the sandflat. This project will generate a comprehensive dietary profile of what this species relies on in these types of habitats. This may help to determine which areas are "hotspots" for juvenile GSRs in other ecological settings. Additionally, gastric lavage is a novel method for use on rays (particularly for juvenile rays). This is the first instance that gastric lavage has been successfully used for stomach content analysis on juvenile rays of this size (<45 cm) which paves the way for future dietary research on rays of similar sizes.
James Cook University, Qld; Dalhousie University, Canada
4287: We have all seen Discovery's Shark Week and Nat Geo's Shark Fest. But how are these shows made? Do they fund science? What are the rights of the scientists featured? With recent changes in access and availability of animals in locations like Bahamas, Mexico and South Africa more productions are looking at Australia and New Zealand as filming locations. This presentation outlines the entire process of documentary making from the initial concept to final delivery and what as a scientist you are entitled to in terms of remuneration and editorial rights. We will present the recommendations and new standards now in place by senior researchers in this process.
4288: Elasmobranchs (sharks and rays) inhabit diverse global habitats, with their distribution boundaries playing a pivotal role in understanding species-specific habitat needs, population status, and ecological dynamics. This is particularly true for species including walking sharks (Hemiscyllium) that exhibit strong site fidelity and habitat associations, making them more susceptible to localised threats including: habitat loss or degradation, harvest and environmental change. Walking sharks consist of 9 species of small, benthic dwelling sharks that are endemic northern Australia, the island of New Guinea and its satellite islands. Three walking shark species are endemic to Papua New Guinea (PNG), with all listed as Vulnerable to Extinction by the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. At present, there are no local or national species-specific protections for walking sharks in PNG and a dearth of information to inform management, with the distributions particularly unclear. Through a series of in-situ surveys, we aim to re-assess the distributional limits of walking sharks in PNG while collecting essential baseline biological and ecological data to benefit the future management of the species. Here we present our preliminary results updating the range limits of two species from PNG (Hemiscyllium michaeli and Hemiscyllium hallstromi) and how these findings will impact ongoing research while benefiting the management of the genus.

4289: Cartilaginous fishes have evolved a skeletal system consisting mainly of unmineralised cartilage, a tissue that resembles mammalian articular cartilage. Yet, little is known about the ability of this tissue to withstand high hydrostatic pressure (HHP), i.e. in deepwater species (200–3000m). In the cartilage of terrestrial mammals, such loads would produce serious mechanical stress resulting in acute tissue damage, suggesting that deepwater chondrichthyans may possess key adaptations in their skeletal system to cope with HHP (20–300atm). This research aims to characterise the extracellular matrix within two skeletal regions in five deepwater species that occupy different depth ranges, to uncover any interspecific differences in the microstructure, composition, and biophysical properties that could explain how they maintain tissue integrity under extreme pressures. The study uses a multimodal approach to cross-correlate histo-morphological data with CT imaging and mechanical testing across species. Our results show marked histological variations in tissue characteristics, such as the level of mineralisation, collagen and proteoglycan contents, and resulting mechanical properties, which may be correlated to depth environments. Ultimately, a better understanding of such adaptations may inform future applications in cartilage tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, in addition to elucidating how some species are able to make large vertical movements within their depth range.

4290: This review explores the integration of network analysis with acoustic telemetry to uncover the complex network structures and behaviors within animal populations. Acoustic telemetry, a pivotal method for monitoring animal movements in their natural habitats, offers detailed spatial and temporal data and, when analyzed through the lens of network analysis, reveals complex network interactions and organization. To explore how merging these approaches offers insights into animal sociology, including hierarchy dynamics, social connectivity, and environmental effects on networks, we discuss methodological foundations, practical applications, and conservation implications, highlighting case studies. The review also addresses the challenges encountered in data collection, analysis, and interpretation, offering potential solutions and emphasizing the importance of technological advancements and collaborative efforts in overcoming these obstacles. Future directions for research are discussed, underscoring the need for more comprehensive studies to further refine and expand our understanding of animal network structures. This work encourages further exploration at the intersection of behavioral ecology, conservation biology, and computational science, aiming to develop innovative conservation strategies and deepen knowledge of animal social lives.

4291: The conservation management of the white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) is intricate due to persistent knowledge gaps in its biology and ecology, particularly regarding the biological connectivity of populations in eastern and southern Australia. This study reassesses population genetic structures using population genomic analyses of approximately 670 individuals genotyped at around 5000 single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) loci. Contrary to previous reports, our analyses reveal a lack of overall genetic structure between sharks from eastern and southern Australia, challenging the notion of discrete biological units. Simulations indicate high connectivity with intergenerational migration rates exceeding 10–30% gene flow. Kinship analyses show numerous first, second, and third-degree relatives between regions, supporting population admixture. The effective population size (Ne) is estimated to be less than 500 individuals, indicating potential risks of inbreeding and fitness declines, particularly among sub-adult sharks. These findings underscore the need for revised national conservation status and spatial management strategies for white sharks in Australia.

4292: White (Carcharodon carcharias) and tiger sharks (Galeocerdo cuvier) are proportionally responsible for the highest fatality from shark bites (26 and 38%, respectively), mostly due to blood loss from vascular lacerations. Puncture-resistant fabrics offer a promising mitigation measure that could reduce the severity of injuries and haemorrhaging, providing additional time for victims to be attended to by emergency services before blood loss becomes fatal. Previous bite-resistant materials are heavy and cumbersome (e.g., chainmail armour), but modern advancements in textile fibre have allowed the development of lightweight alternatives incorporated into traditional wetsuits. We tested the efficacy of four novel bite-resistant fabrics to reduce damage from white and tiger shark bites. Ninety bites from each species were collected on "bite packages" with a neoprene pouch covering a wooden panel wrapped in two sheets of vinyl acetate foam. Damage from bites on these fabrics were compared to control bites on a regular 3-mm neoprene. Although slight differences between fabrics were observed, all four bite-resistant fabrics decreased substantial damage (large tear where foam has been removed) while increasing the area of bites that remained undamaged. Our findings show that lightweight bite-resistant wetsuit fabrics may be a beneficial personal mitigation measure to reduce damage from white and tiger shark bites.

4293: Over the last 500 million years, vertebrates have gone through several major evolutionary changes, including the origin of jaws, the acquisition of paired fins and the transition from fins to limbs. By exploring the differences in developmental networks across the vertebrate phylogeny we can begin to understand how these evolutionary changes may have occurred. Historically the main model systems in developmental biology have been mice, chick and zebrafish. Using the epaulette shark as a representative Chondrichthyan provides a unique and ancient anchor for comparisons with these traditional model species. Chondrichthyans are the oldest group of extant jawed vertebrates, branching off over 400 million years ago. The epaulette shark is a small, oviparous shark, well known for its ability to 'walk' on its fins and adaptability to captive life. At Monash University, we have a breeding colony of epaulette sharks which aid in our research of vertebrate body plan evolution. There are relatively few resources for studying the development of sharks, but our breeding facility contributes to expanding those resources with experimental tools and techniques, a comprehensive staging guide and Whole Genome Sequencing. This presentation will briefly cover some key aspects of managing a captive breeding colony, and show examples from our comprehensive staging guide. The staging guide will provide a detailed view of developmental morphologies using live images and MicroCT data sets.

4294: The white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) is a highly migratory species and is known to regularly form aggregations in key locations globally, with the Neptune Islands being recognised as the largest and most significant aggregation site for adult white sharks in Australia. Here seasonal white shark aggregations appear to be resource driven and associated with prey abundance. However, monitoring programs point to differences in seasonal habitat usage between individuals and the possibility of additional drivers influencing aggregation behaviours. In this study, we investigated the possibility of aggregation patterns and community structure among white sharks at the Neptune Islands being genetically determined and linked to underlying patterns of relatedness between individual sharks via the use of a kinship analyses derived from a high-density panel of SNP genomic loci. Relatedness measures were then integrated with metadata associated with aggregation site use, inferred from acoustic tag data and a photographic identification register, for analytical purposes. This presentation will provide an overview of the findings from these analyses and the implications of our results with respect to understanding white shark biology and ecology and the management of white sharks in the Neptune Islands.

4295: A profound knowledge on the stress physiology of sharks is pivotal to inform and refine future conservation efforts, especially considering that many stressors will increase both in frequency and severity over the coming decades. However, directed studies on the physiological stress response in sharks are rare. In this study, by applying an experimental stress paradigm, we tested the hypotheses that chronic stress (1) positively correlates with a shark's aerobic capacity to assist in oxygen debt recovery, (2) positively correlates with energy mobilisation to combat stress, and (3) negatively correlates with the sharks' fitness as a result of an increased energetic demand to restore homeostasis. We found no significant changes in oxygen-carrying capacity (i.e., haematocrit, haemoglobin), minimum oxygen uptake rates, and glucose concentration (a conventional vertebrate stress biomarker) in neonatal blacktip reef sharks (C. melanopterus) throughout our 50-days experiment or between stress treatments. Our data did, however, show a decline in growth rate and body condition with chronic stress, for the first time demonstrating how stress reflects changes that could compromise fitness. Additionally, our state-of-the-art discovery metabolomics approach uncovered an increased mobilisation of glutamine with chronic stress. As such, this amino acids may be a long-sought chronic stress biomarker for sharks, which may have wide-reaching applications for shark management and conservation.

4296: Environmental changes and phenotypic responses are directly linked through epigenetics - the cellular mechanism that switches genes on or off. In natural populations, the ability to rapidly change gene-expression determines how a species can cope with environmental extremes. Such plastic responses are crucial for populations to persist in the initial stages of adaptation. Here, we focus on DNA methylation of CpG dinucleotides, one of the main epigenetic modifications in vertebrates. We measured methylation changes in School Sharks (Galeorhinus galeus) that were subjected to different experimental conditions and examined (epi)genetic variation in natural populations. We sequenced 127 School Sharks to characterize 1.2 million CpG sites and 45,000 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). In juvenile sharks subjected to acute thermal and salinity stress, we identified 208 CpG sites associated with these environmental stressors, indicating rapid methylation changes can provide a buffer to acute stress. Subsequently, we investigated these stress-related methylation patterns in natural population to understand if animals in the wild show similar responses. We also studied the stability of methylation between tissue types and quantified the population-level variation. Overall, the study provides estimates of methylation and nucleotide diversity as a proxy for the adaptive potential of populations and highlight the use of epigenetic sequencing to monitor climate stress in wild animals.

4297: Since 2012, our team has studied the epaulette shark (Hemiscyllium ocellatum), an ideal subject for laboratory experiments and field studies, endemic to the Great Barrier Reef. Through our established breeding colony, we have conducted extensive studies on all life stages and responses to anthropogenic stressors with global partnerships. Initial studies focused on elevated CO2 responses, revealing key physiological traits required future ocean acidification tolerance. Unaffected foraging and sheltering behaviours were observed, even in embryonic and juvenile stages. Subsequent studies shifted to the impacts of elevated temperatures, reflecting this shark's natural habitat extremes. We found smaller embryos hatched earlier, with reduced aerobic scope, faster energy utilization, delayed post-exercise recovery, and altered colouration. Elevated temperatures also altered muscle growth, decreased growth rates, and increased mortality in hatchlings, indicating climate change vulnerability throughout early ontogeny. Our current research explores traits crucial for the species' adaptation to acute and ongoing warming. This research highlights the epaulette shark as a vital model for studying climate change impacts on physiology, genetics, and behaviour in an evolutionarily old group. Epaulette sharks' unique traits and vulnerability to climate change make them excellent for engaging the public in discussions on conservation and marine biodiversity in our rapidly changing world.

4298: The global number of shark bites has increased over the past four decades with, however, high regional variability both in space and time. A plethora of causative factors have been proposed to explain these patterns, but the infrequent nature of human-shark interactions makes it difficult to determine the underlying causes of these events. Our systematic review, aligned with the 2020 PRISMA guidelines, explores peer-reviewed literature published between 1960 and 2023 to identify factors potentially explaining trends in human-shark interactions and quantify research efforts. We identified 60 publications, mainly from six global shark bite hotspots — the United States, South Africa, Australia, Brazil, Reunion Island, and New-Caledonia. These studies suggest that variations in the frequency of human-shark interactions could be explained by a range of factors, including changes in prey availability, environmental conditions, human and shark population density and behavior, as well as habitat destruction. However, only five studies have conducted statistical assessments of their impact. The increased number in human-shark interactions and the frequent clusters of shark bites within short timeframes offer new opportunities to test the causative factors that may explain trends in unprovoked shark bites. Enhancing our understanding of the factors contributing to shark bites is essential for improving risk reduction policies for humans and conservation plans for shark populations.

4299: Shallow water habitat use by young reef sharks has long been attributed to high food availability and low predation risk, facilitating rapid growth and survival. However, little is understood about the risk of predation within these areas. Using drone footage, two measures of predation risk (spatial overlap and encounter rate with predators) of young blacktip reef sharks, Carcharhinus melanopterus, and their reef predators (i.e., older conspecifics) were quantified in five terrestrial reef flats of Mo'orea, French Polynesia. Overall, we found little evidence of temporal partitioning of space as consistent measures of predation risk were observed across a diel cycle. While we found a consistent risk of predation across all surveyed sites, spatial overlap between young blacktips and their predators was greater in areas with high benthic habitat complexity. This was potentially due to an increase in shared food resources in complex habitats (i.e., teleost fish and crustaceans). Additionally, spatial overlap between young blacktips and their reef predators was disproportionate to the observed predator-prey encounter rates, indicating that external factors may limit the possible number of encounters from what would be expected by spatial overlap alone. We suggest that young blacktips remain in terrestrial reef flats despite regular interactions with predators through relying on their ability to out-manoeuvre their larger predators in these shallow complex environments.

4300: Essential habitats are areas which critically underpin the survival of species through one or multiple life stages. Although general habitat use has been broadly studied for tiger sharks, Galeocerdo cuvier, very little is understood about habitat use by neonate and young of the year sharks (YOY). Here, we aimed to identify essential habitats for juvenile tiger sharks, while assessing potential pupping grounds along the Queensland coast. We utilised multidecadal catch data from the shark control program to assess the prevalence of juveniles along the Queensland coast, and conducted targeted fishing surveys in the Palm and Whitsunday Islands. Cairns and Townsville regions had higher catches of juveniles relative to other locations on the coast. Research fishing surveys found a marked difference in juvenile (<2m TL) relative abundance between the Palm Islands (CPUE = 0.14 sharks per hook hours), and the Whitsundays at (CPUE = 0.0 sharks per hook hours). Acoustic tracking of sharks in the Palm Islands showed subadult/adult sharks (>2m TL) tended to have higher residency index, averaging at 0.0690, whereas smaller sharks (<2m TL) were much lower, at 0.0070. To date, Townsville and Cairns appear to be the most likely regions containing essential habitats for juvenile tiger sharks. To further explore this, additional targeted fishing surveys and tagging will be conducted over the next year in areas between Cairns and Townsville, including the Palm Island group.

4301: Fishing activities pose the primary threat to deepwater chondrichthyans (sharks, rays, and chimaeras). These species are highly susceptible to overexploitation but are frequently captured as bycatch. While international interest in understanding and reducing fishing mortality on chondrichthyans is growing, limited research has been conducted on deepwater species. In January 2024, at-vessel mortality and capture stress under normal fishing conditions were measured for deepwater chondrichthyans on Chatham Rise, New Zealand. At-vessel mortality and physical condition were assessed for 1301 unique specimens, representing 31 species and 15 families. A random subset of 247 specimens from 19 species were temporarily housed in an 800 L tank for up to 12h to monitor their health, evaluate capture stress and estimate short-term post-release mortality rates. A range of indicators related to physical (general condition and organ-specific examinations), behavioural (responses to stimuli and stress-related behaviours), and physiological status through blood analysis (blood-gas, acid-base, haematology, blood chemistry, and hormones) were collected. In total, 1627 physical and behavioural assessments were completed, and 471 blood samples collected. An overview of the sampling protocols, data collection, and future research plans will be presented.

4302: Understanding the behavioral responses of marine megafauna to anthropogenic disturbances is crucial for effective conservation management. To understand the effect of human aquatic recreation on manta ray behavior we employed aerial drone surveys to investigate the flight responses of reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) in response to in-water human activity. Through coordinated UAS (drone) surveys conducted in a known manta ray habitat we analyzed the influence of human recreation choices on the flight responses of M. alfredi. Aerial drone technology offers a non-invasive approach, enabling the collection of high-resolution imagery and behavioral data over large spatial scales. The integration of drone technology in marine conservation strategies offers a promising avenue for assessing and mitigating human-induced impacts on marine megafauna. Preliminary findings suggest correlations between specific anthropogenic parameters and manta ray flight behaviors. These insights provide a foundation for developing management guidelines to protect M. alfredi populations while permitting ecotourism and aquatic recreation to coexist. Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader understanding of the ecological dynamics of reef manta rays and provides valuable tools for conservation practitioners to implement targeted management measures aimed at minimizing disturbance and ensuring the sustainable coexistence of M. alfredi with human activities in their natural habitats.

4303: The isiMangaliso Wetland Park is a large multi-use MPA along the east coast of South Africa. The area encompasses the southernmost coral reef systems of Africa and exhibits an extraordinarily high elasmobranch diversity. Due to its large size, the different management zonations within, and the presence of various habitats, the area represents a unique opportunity to investigate elasmobranch communities and the underlying factors governing their distributions and compositions. Furthermore, the marginal nature of the ecosystems necessitates a thorough understanding of local population dynamics and space use, as southward-expansions of population ranges are foreseeable due to climate change. The herein presented research project encompasses seasonality, diel shifts, MPA zonation, and the importance of habitat characteristics in shaping elasmobranch communities, with special focus on oceanographic features. Data is collected using BRUVs and a novel method of eDNA collection which aims to reduce replicate variability and increase detectability. As I am still in the early phase of my PhD, I have only sampled one season so far – two seasons by the time the conference takes place. Nonetheless, certain patterns are already manifesting, such as higher diversity/abundance near submarine canyons, reef structural complexity only playing a role for certain species, and the eDNA samples detecting species which have not yet been reported in the park.
4304: Ocean warming threatens all marine ecosystems with observed and predicted shifts in animal movements, range extensions, and changes in movement patterns documented across marine taxa. Understanding how threatened species, such as white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias), may respond to climate change contributes to the effective management and conservation of this vulnerable species. Ensuring that management approaches are responsive to changes in climate, species distributions, and habitat change can assist with the long-term survival of this species. Satellite Position Only Tags (SPOT) were deployed on 64 white sharks over 9-years (2015–2019) on the east coast of Australia from Forster to Lennox head, New South Whales. We used benthos type, bathymetry, and sea surface temperature to build a machine-learning resource selection function model to identify patterns in habitat selection and predict white shark occurrence in response to ocean warming. We determined that white sharks preferentially select sandy-bottomed habitats within 13 – 20 °C. While analysis is ongoing, our study will demonstrate the power of machine learning techniques to predict changes in habitat suitability and species distribution in the face of climate change.

4305: Environmental fluctuations can drive changes in animal behaviour, triggering annual migrations for food, optimal weather, or reproduction, as well as short-term activity changes. Using acoustic accelerometer tags deployed on over 600 white (Carcharodon carcharias) sharks from 2020 to 2024, we explored how environmental conditions (i.e., temperature, tides, moon phase and time of day) influence the activity of sharks in Eastern Australian waters. We identified that white sharks were more active between 1800 and 2400 at lower latitudes (-25 to -30 °S) and most active between 1000 and 1400 at higher latitudes (-40 °S). Wind direction was the primary factor driving white shark activity levels, with shark activity increasing in northwest winds likely due to calmer seas. In contrast, southeast winds, often associated with rougher seas, saw a decrease in white shark activity. This study will be used to inform shark management programs and the public of environmental factors that increase white shark activity and certain times of day, locations, and environmental conditions that may increase the risk of shark encounters.

4306: Along the coast of south-eastern Australia, ocean temperatures are increasing at a rapid rate, but our understanding of temperate elasmobranch shifts in distributions and abundance in relation to these environmental changes is limited, and the extent to which marine protected areas (MPAs) offer protection is lacking. This research, located along Victoria, Australia, aimed to investigate habitat and environmental associations to predict elasmobranch species distributions and abundance now and into the future and determine the effectiveness of MPAs on protecting populations of elasmobranchs under current and future environmental conditions. Using a dataset of 1,048 baited remote underwater video stations (BRUVS), observations of six elasmobranch species abundances and elasmobranch richness, we developed generalised additive models (GAMs) to associate those observations with environmental drivers including satellite and model derived oceanographic variables and seafloor habitat. We found SST and wave energy to be the main environmental drivers of abundance and that future changes in those variables were likely to drive decreases in populations of 45 – 75% and MPAs protect varying levels of predicted populations with proportional protection increasing into the future.

4307: Shark ecotourism is a non-extractive alternative to fishing with capacity to generate revenue, offer employment, and support conservation. Little is known about the spatial ecology of common coastal sharks in Hawaiʻi, even the most abundant species encountered at Oʻahu ecotourism sites. I am investigating how these shark populations are responding to the growing number of ecotourism operations (2 in 2007; >15 in 2023) by assessing historical (2007-2018) and contemporary (2019-2023) movements, residency and abundance of sharks associated with these sites. From 2019-2023, I tagged 38 Galapagos, sandbar and tiger sharks at ecotourism sites to compare their movements with 47 sharks tagged at these sites from 2007-2009;2014. Preliminary analyses show sharks captured at ecotourism sites visit these sites regularly but range widely around Oʻahu and beyond. These ecotour-tagged sharks show clear diel behavior patterns, associating with moorings by day, roaming further afield at night. There is evidence of contiguous seasonal migrations by sharks in the number of sharks detected at ecotourism sites. 53 sharks tagged at distant locations were detected at ecotourism sites occasionally passed through the area remaining for a few minutes or a few days. Analyses are ongoing to determine whether shark residency is increasing over time at these sites. This data will fill key knowledge gaps about shark ecology. These results will facilitate science driven management of shark ecotourism.

4308: Most ecological studies focus on top predators and their influences on lower trophic levels or on basal primary producers that structure marine ecosystems. Mesopredators receive less attention but outnumber top predators in both biomass and number of species, and play essentials roles in linking upper and lower trophic levels. Shifts in ecosystems dynamics, partly driven by changing climates and declines in the abundance of top marine predators might lead to mesopredators becoming more prevalent and to broadening their trophic role due to increased competition. Characterisation of niche width and overlap can help better understand resource use, whereby narrow and wide niche width can be indicative of specialist or generalist feeding, respectively. Niche overlap can be an indicator of shared resources or competition. Here, I use fatty acids and stable isotopes to inform diet and calculate niche width and overlap of 16 sympatric Chondrichthyes to estimate resource sharing and identify generalist and specialist feeders. Muscle fatty acids revealed significant differences in diet between all species, and grouping into three distinct clusters; pelagic feeders, reef-demersal feeders, and deep-demersal feeders. It is imperative to understand resource partitioning as there is a growing concern that due to declining top-predator abundance and subsequent mesopredator release, the trophic roles of chondrichthyan mesopredators will shift, changing food web structure along with it.
4309: Acoustic telemetry often involves an invasive method of internal tagging, wherein the animal is incised, a transmitter internally inserted into the coelomic cavity, after which the incision is closed with sutures to aid wound closure, healing, and tag retention. However, the stitching of the wound can be time-consuming especially when field conditions are not optimal, leading to additional handling stress, which can be fatal in sensitive species or extreme cases. We assessed whether animal welfare of internally-tagged sharks can be improved by reducing handling time through keeping incision wounds unsutured. A 63-day captive study measured physical (i.e., macroscopic assessment of incision healing progress), bacterial dynamics (i.e., colony forming units), physiological (i.e., cortisol levels), and histological (i.e., cell type and morphology) responses to two internal acoustic transmitter tagging procedures (i.e., with and without sutures) in twelve Port Jackson (Heterodontus portusjacksoni) sharks. Sutures facilitated fast wound closure but led to greater inflammation compared to unsutured incisions. Sutured incisions also had ~100 times more colony forming units present than unsutured incisions, despite the use of autoclaved surgical tools. Tag retention was 100% in both treatments and incisions were, on average, completely healed by ~14 days, but unsutured incisions healed slower. Our study contributes to our understanding of elasmobranch healing and tagging effects.

4310: Marine animals rely on their epidermal microbiomes (resident communities of bacteria and viruses) to eliminate pathogens and avoid infection. The virome, comprised of viruses and bacteriophages, is critical to marine epidermal microbiome defense systems. Sharks demonstrate a unique resistance to epidermal infections despite frequent injury and exposure to opportunistic pathogens. Shark epidermal immunity stems in part from innate mechanisms, such as skin morphology, immune responses, and antimicrobial secretions, but the role of the epidermal virome in shark health is an outstanding question. We sampled the epidermis of sharks from the southwestern Pacific, including white (Carcharodon carcharias), tiger (Galeocerdo cuvier), dusky (Carcharhinus obscurus), and sandbar (Carcharhinus plumbeus) sharks (total n=43). Some individuals had epidermal lesions at various healing stages (n=5), which were sampled along with nearby undamaged skin. Viral abundance was estimated using flow cytometry. Wounded skin harbored over 10-fold higher abundance of virus-like particles (VLPs) compared to undamaged skin on the same individual, and higher VLP abundance than undamaged conspecifics. To investigate this phenomenon experimentally, epidermal viral abundance was estimated on captive Port Jackson sharks (Heterodontus portusjacksoni, n=10) with healing surgical wounds, sampled prior to incision and at 7-day intervals for 21 days post-incision. Here we present the results of that experiment.

4311: Vertebrate cartilage possesses limited regenerative abilities in responding to injuries and degeneration due to sudden and/or extreme load exposure as well as medical conditions such as arthritis. Extreme loads are borne by chondrichthyan fishes thriving in environments from shallow water (< 200m) to deep water (> 200m) of up to 3,000m. While many extant species live at these depths or migrate between different zones of the water column, the mechanisms they have evolved to withstand and adapt to constant and/or varying hydrostatic pressures are unknown. To investigate whether any key biological adaptations to constant/varying extreme hydrostatic pressures are present, this study assesses two skeletal regions (cranium and vertebra) across four devil ray species (n = 2) that show frequent vertical movements. Preliminary results are compared with five deepwater chondrichthyan species (n = 2) that never (or only seasonally) surface. Using a multi-scale approach, the research aims to characterise 1) the histological organisation, composition, and architecture of un-mineralised and mineralised cartilage and 2) the mechanical properties of these tissues and their interfaces. This comparative approach will help to build a baseline knowledge of the composition and arrangement of cartilage and extracellular matrix that has naturally evolved to withstand high hydrostatic pressures and will inform future research in cartilage tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, and biomimetics.

4312: Animal aggregations are common and often driven by resource availability and synchrony of daily or seasonal activity. However, information on aggregation ecology is limited for many species, including the white shark (Carcharodon carcharias), where the Neptune Islands is one of Australia's largest shark aggregation sites. Non-random associations of four communities suggest that factors other than prey abundance might influence aggregatory patterns. This study aimed to determine whether the co-occurrence of individual sharks, and variation in visitation patterns, is influenced by relatedness, a known driver of aggregation in other animal systems. To achieve this, 133 white sharks were genotyped at 5,000 SNP loci using reduced genome representation sequencing. Relatedness amongst shark pairs was determined using a combination of co-ancestry coefficients and likelihood approaches, and tests for correlations between shark relatedness and location, degree of residency and seasonality were conducted. Analyses indicated low levels of relatedness among pairs and no significant relationship between genetic relatedness and location, degree of residency or seasonality of shark visitation. This study shows that relatedness is not likely to be a factor influencing visitation and shark co-occurrence, highlighting the need for further research to identifying alternative drivers of aggregatory patterns at the Neptune Islands to help inform future management of this key marine predator.

4313: Our understanding of the trophic role of elasmobranchs is often limited and can be attributed to the difficulty in obtaining sufficient sample sizes and material. Tissues alongside jaws are often stored in a range of chemical preservatives or frozen for long-term keepsake or to reach a desired appearance by researchers, museums or private collectors. If we are to use preserved jaws for dietary studies, we must first understand the impacts jaw preservation methods have on carbon, nitrogen and sulphur stable isotopes of elasmobranch teeth. This remains a major limitation, curtailing the use samples from museum and private collections. We assessed if chemical preservation affected tooth stable isotopes of three different elasmobranch species when freshly preserved, or after six months, and if this impact varies among different tooth morphologies. Findings showed that there was no impact of preservation on tooth stable isotopes. Impact on the biochemistry of the tooth samples was also noted to be potentially affected by the amount of tissue processed and analysed. Ongoing sample processing and analysis aims to provide further explanations to the variability seen in the preliminary findings. By understanding how preservation impacts stable isotopes of elasmobranch teeth, preserved jaws from museum or private collections will become available and complement samples from fresh jaws to study the trophic ecology of elasmobranchs.

4314: The Slender Bambooshark (Chiloscyllium indicum) is a common Indo-West Pacific species at risk from increasing fishing pressure and coastal development. Though wide ranging within the region, little is known about the ecology of this small mesopredator. We tagged 10 sharks with acoustic transmitters to investigate movement within an area in the Johor Strait between Singapore and Malaysia. Preliminary results indicate that at this site these small, benthic, sharks exhibit diel patterns of movement from deeper areas within a shipping channel, to shallower coastal areas. Tracking data of up to 400+ days for some individuals indicates that home-ranges are small. While this may mean that populations are particularly vulnerable to human impacts at a local scale, conversely it also suggests that spatial management of relatively small areas could be a valuable approach to protecting this vulnerable species.
4315: Many elasmobranchs, including shark-like rays, play a complex role in maintaining the balance in marine food webs. They prey on a wide range of marine organisms and occupy a range of apex and meso-predatory roles that maintain the stability of marine food webs. This study aims to investigate Critically Endangered Wedgefish (Rhynchobatus spp.) diet in the Indo-West Pacific region based on geography, seasonal pattern, size, and sex class. To date, data collection from Southwest Aceh and Northern Java, Indonesia, between October 2023 and February 2024, consists of 47 individuals from three species (R. australiae, R. laevis and R. springeri show wedgefish diet items, including Mollusca (Class Cephalopoda and Bivalvia), Crustacea (Order Decapoda and Infraorder Brachyura), Teleostei (Family Ballistidae, Mullidae, Genus Namipterus and Priyacantus tayenus). Further step to acquire more accurate results include using environmental DNA analysis that have become increasingly popular as a sensitive, non-invasive technique for dietary assessments.

4316: Large predatory elasmobranchs are vital components of marine ecosystems, largely via top-down control of meso-predator and prey abundance and presence. The tiger shark, Galeocerdo cuvier, is one of a few larger elasmobranch species along the eastern Australian coast fulfilling this top tier role. The large-scale movement of individuals plays an important role in trophic links connecting distant and distinct coastal and pelagic ecosystems. Despite this there are some glaring gaps in species' ecological and biological knowledge in published data resulting from a lack of adult male tiger sharks in movement analysis and subsequent conclusions. From targeted capture and deployment of satellite tags onto adult male tiger sharks, male-specific movement has been captured. Here we show that as with other animals, tiger sharks exhibit sex-biased movement that may play a major role in survival strategies and biological functions. While juveniles and adult female tiger sharks exhibit distinct trends in migration times and fine-scale diel movement, adult males are potentially utilizing different pathways and cues for movement and behaviour. While previously presumed, the implications of identifying sex-related movement allows for further analysis that may provide insight into biological and ecological interactions, such as location of mating grounds or indirect versus direct pressure among ecosystems.

4317: The pyjama shark is a Scyliorhinid species endemic to South Africa. Even though it is kept in captivity in many aquaria, there is a lack of research on its growth and development. In this study, we investigated the fertilization rate of eggs and the age at female sexual maturation in captive sharks and compared their growth to that of wild individuals. This is the first study to compare the growth of captive and wild catsharks as well as the first study to compare growth in male and female pyjama sharks. The mean incubation rate (±standard error of the mean [SE]) was 239.46 ± 4.97 days, the mean Lt of hatchlings (±SE) was 14.65 ± 0.24 cm, and the mean Wt (±SE) was 17.19 ± 0.75 g. One female laid fertilized eggs 6.6 years after hatching and was considered sexually mature. Both in captivity and in the wild, males showed negative allometric growth and females showed isometric growth. The growth performance (Φ') was also greater in captive sharks compared to wild sharks regardless of sex. However, there was significant variation in growth between individuals of the same sex. The similar growth patterns found in wild and captive populations are a very useful tool for informing future conservation management if the population of this shark species were to decline in the future and also prove that captive studies for this species are transferable to wild populations with regard to sexual differences.

4318: Noise pollution in the ocean has been increasing by nearly three decibels every ten years, causing a disruption in a previously serene acoustic environment. The Australian ghost shark, Callorhinchus milii, migrates from great depths to reproduce in shallow waters and is predicted to rely heavily on its hearing, as indicated by the size and unique specialisations of its ears. We aim to determine the possible impacts of anthropogenic noise on the development of the auditory system of C. milii. Captive embryos were exposed during their entire development to two acoustic conditions: an ambient soundscape or boat noise. Embryos and hatchlings were collected at different timepoints, preserved and scanned using micro-computed tomography. The nervous system, including the morphology of the hearing apparatus and the brain, will be compared between treatments by quantifying the volume, size and shape of the inner ear compared to controls throughout development. This is the first study investigating the impact of noise on the development of any chondrichthyan species. Our research will establish, for the first time, an overlooked but potentially severe threat to an important group of cartilaginous fishes.

4319: Reef sharks have experienced widespread declines across much of the world's coral reefs as a result of decades of overexploitation. Large knowledge gaps concerning the abundance of reef sharks worldwide have limited effective restoration and management of coastal shark populations. Although recent research has assessed the global status and conservation potential of reef sharks, causal questions remain regarding the effects of current management strategies. Using data from baited remote underwater video systems (BRUVS) from 371 sampling locations across 58 nations globally, we implemented a causal inference framework to determine cause-and-effect relationships between direct management actions and reef shark abundance. We developed Bayesian hierarchical models comprised of regional, national, reef, and set spatial scales to quantify the effect of shark sanctuaries, marine protected areas, and fishing restrictions on the relative abundance of reef sharks. Counterfactual scenarios in which different management interventions are implemented at each reef were used to determine the net benefit of management actions at the national level based on expected changes in shark abundance and the likelihood of management action. Here, we highlight the power of causal inference in understanding ecological relationships beyond the capabilities of predictive techniques typically used with observational data and evaluate management-related drivers of global reef shark abundance.

4320: As most people will not encounter sharks in the wild, the media's portrayal of these animals contributes to public perception and conservation support. Therefore, understanding how sharks are portrayed in the media is important for shark conservation research. This poster presents findings from various studies exploring sharks in the media and the impact of media portrayals on public perception. Through analysing 2,643 shark-related Facebook posts made by Australian news media outlets during 2016 it was found that 87% of all the news-related Facebook pages published at least one post related to sharks and only 49 days in 2016 had no published shark-related posts. Through analysing 109 shark films it was found that almost all of these films (96%) overtly portrayed shark-human interactions as being potentially threatening to humans and only one film did not include potentially threatening interactions. Further, when investigating animal related horror films more broadly, sharks were found to be the most depicted animal. To begin to understand the impact of these portrayals, a mixed-method experiment found that people's perception of risk of sharks significantly increased after viewing shark related news headlines. Since public perception of shark mitigation can motivate politicians to fund and support shark management and conservation, it is important that research continues to explore the impact of media portrayal of sharks and peoples' fear and acceptance of sharks broadly.
4321: Shark vertebrae are biogeochemical archives of environmental conditions and are proving to be a valuable tool in determining life history traits. We here investigate the use and inter-complementary of high spatial resolution spectroscopy, X-Ray spectrometry and mass-spectrometry techniques to unravel the sclerochronological life records. Thin sections of four elasmobranch species were examined through a range of instruments including Raman, μXRF, LA-ICP-MS, and high-resolution SIMS (SHRIMP). High-definition maps and transect analyses were amalgamated to produce interpretable, reliable data images. Through Raman spectroscopy the nature of cartilage crystallisation to bioapatite was captured, allowing the nature of sequential modelling of the vertebra to be analysed. Elemental maps (μXRF, LA-ICP-MS) provided insights into the concentrations of minor and trace elements capturing patterns of seasonality within the chronological structure. These maps may provide more accurate ways to age sharks, particularly for species that are notoriously difficult to age. In-situ oxygen isotopes were also determined to gain further insights into migratory species that have a show buffered or no elemental variation. These analyses provide a preliminary insight and a baseline for further investigation into the usefulness of shark vertebrae as a sclerochronological tool to better understand and manage these animals that are critical to the stability and health of our ecosystems.

4322: Current elasmobranch ageing methods often leave sharks systematically underaged, having severe management implications, and impacting demographic analysis and estimation of population recovery rates. Validating ageing techniques and enhancing our ability to infer habitat use across ages is fundamental to proper management. The growth mechanisms of shark vertebrae and the incorporation of trace elements (and their isotopic signatures) into the internal structure of vertebrae are poorly understood. Further, the extent of the information that can be gathered by analysing trace elements along the growth axis of vertebrae is still developing. To find a more reliable ageing technique that removes ambiguity and seeks to validate conventional methods (optical microscopy), vertebrae from pelagic, coastal and riverine species have been selected and analysed to discriminate the presence of elemental variations in their vertebrae using SEM-EDS, EPMA, μXRF, LA-ICP-MS and LA-MC-ICP-MS. It was found that elemental distribution varied significantly between species from different habitat types, and variances were more pronounced in coastal and riverine species that are exposed to terrigenous runoff. We find that μXRF effectively improved the visibility of ageing structures, and expressed patterns based on seasonality, further supported by radiogenic Sr isotopic ratios (87Sr/86Sr by LA-MC-ICP-MS) and may prove a more accurate way to age sharks.

4323: The nocturnal ecology of elasmobranchs has often been overlooked due to the logistical challenges of conducting nocturnal surveys. However, the rise in technologically advantageous survey techniques, such as remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), demonstrates the potential to circumnavigate these challenges. Through pilot surveys on the Great Barrier Reef, this study investigated the strengths and limitations of using underwater ROVs to gather nocturnal data on elasmobranchs. Diver performed Underwater visual census (UVC) and ROV surveying techniques were compared along 100-meter transects, during daylight, twilight, and night hours. Night surveys using ROVs were conducted with alternating red and white lights to test the potential influences of introducing light into a dark environment. Although technical improvements were identified to improve performance, elasmobranchs were most often observed by the ROV and at nighttime. Overall, ROVs demonstrate potential as highly viable and logistically advantageous alternatives for repetitive transect surveys on the reef.

4324: Tiger sharks are wide-ranging predators that remain resident to specific areas seasonally in the South Pacific Ocean, presumably due to factors associated with foraging, reproduction, physiology, or a combination thereof. The contribution of these factors towards movement decisions is not well understood — knowledge of which can help identify potential impacts from changing environmental conditions or manage human-shark interactions. Our study explores the relative importance of abiotic factors affecting the movements of tiger sharks from a relatively small-scale during summer aggregations at Norfolk Island, Australia, to their expansive movements across the western South Pacific. Sharks were tracked with either acoustic (n = 42 individuals) or satellite (n = 35 individuals) telemetry between 2020 and 2023. Movements around Norfolk Island were focused on the west side of the island, likely in response to a known scavenging site associated with butcher waste disposal or to a wedge-tailed shearwater colony. At a larger scale, habitat suitability modelling indicated that distance from the nearest land was the most important variable with some influence of sea surface temperature and bathymetry, but independent of chlorophyll levels and bathymetrical slope, across all months of the year. Both small- and large-scale findings highlight reliance on being close to land throughout their movements, potentially as a method to optimise access to food sources originating from land.

4325: The millions of data that have been collected on the movement and space use of sharks and rays worldwide have been crucial in advancing knowledge of the complex interactions that occur within aquatic ecosystems and have helped identify critical conservation gaps and facilitate effective management strategies. Nevertheless, research output across studies, systems, or even species are often not readily findable, accessible, interoperable, or reusable (FAIR) hindering the prioritisation and optimisation of research and management impact. Here, we introduce TrackdAT, an open-source online portal that hosts metadata from over 2500 peer-reviewed acoustic telemetry articles worldwide. Using TrackdAT, we highlight >350 studies tracking >100 species of sharks and rays and summarize common trends in study topics, objectives, findings, and overall impact. Furthermore, we explore spatial and temporal patterns in shark and ray tracking research in Oceania and globally. We illustrate how acoustic telemetry research has broadened our ecological knowledge of species interactions, critical habitats, timing and spatial extent of movements, ontogenetic shifts, and spawning behaviour of chondrichthyans. We also demonstrate the utility of TrackdAT for identifying gaps in existing research, mobilizing knowledge at regional and global scales, encouraging stakeholder engagement, and optimizing the future of tracking research for sharks and rays.

4326: Sharks and rays are increasingly threatened due to overexploitation, prompting international conservation efforts such as species and genus-specific listings on Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). We investigated the discrepancies between reported catch data for CITES-listed shark species from publicly available databases for catches and international trade. We found substantial disparities between reported catches and documented trade of CITES-listed shark species. This suggests underreporting and/or misreporting within one or more of the databases analysed. Factors contributing to these discrepancies may include inadequate monitoring and reporting mechanisms, misclassifications of species, low levels of data resolution, and lack of communication and cohesiveness between international bodies' databases. Understanding the root causes of these discrepancies is crucial for effective conservation and fisheries management. Improved collaboration and data sharing between bodies monitoring catch, particularly in Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (ABNJs) and CITES will enhance the accuracy of information on shark catch and trade, enabling more informed conservation policies and enforcement measures. In addition to results of the catch and trade database comparisons, recommendations for improved monitoring and data acquisition will be presented.

4327: Globally, whale shark (Rhincodon typus) conservation is guided by research at aggregation sites. However, with only sporadic sightings reported, the east coast of Australia (including the Coral Sea) remains a black hole in terms of whale shark knowledge. To address this knowledge gap, we overlayed historical sightings data (from anecdotal reports, public databases, and aerial surveys) with environmental/oceanographic information, aiming at identifying potential aggregation sites. Wreck Bay in the far northern GBR was identified as the most likely aggregation site during monsoon season. Since 2018, three field trips were conducted to this area, involving aerial surveys, satellite tagging, and photo identification. Here, we present the first species distribution model for the region. This model integrates recent satellite tracking data, historical sightings, and a suit of environmental variables to establish a detailed understanding of habitat suitability and movement patterns in the region. The model confirms that the Wreck Bay area is an essential habitat to whale sharks and identifies other potentially important sites. We also present preliminary demographic insights, shedding light on the population structure. Our findings fill a critical knowledge gap in whale shark research not only for the Coral Sea, but also for the broader Asia/West Pacific region. Results will contribute to regional population estimates, with implications for global conservation initiatives.

4328: The Queensland SharkSmart drone trial was established in September 2020 to investigate the effectiveness of drones as a shark bite mitigation tool in Queensland conditions. Drones provide real-time monitoring of sharks at 10 popular beach locations, with nine in Southeast Queensland and one in North Queensland. The program has flown over 15,000 flights, covering >6,000 km. There have been >500 sightings of sharks, with ~30% estimated to be >2 m in length. On average, sharks are sighted on 3% of flights, highlighting the low risk posed to ocean users. Highest sighting rates have occurred at North Stradbroke Island and Burleigh Beach on the Gold Coast, with lowest sightings at Alexandra Headland Beach on the Sunshine Coast. Statistical analysis indicated that location, the presence of other fauna, season and time of day were the most important factors influencing shark sightings. Heatmaps of shark activity have been generated from tracks of shark movements, to identify fine-scale spatial use, thus informing risk levels for ocean users. The drone trial has provided added safety benefits through assisting with rescues and missing person searches and has contributed a wealth of footage and data on other megafauna. Upcoming trials of Artificial Intelligence algorithms and advanced camera technologies seek to further improve the detection capabilities in the trial and the safety of ocean users.

4329: Zooplankton are important in ocean ecosystems as they link primary productivity to higher trophic levels. Large planktivores such as reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) rely on zooplankton productivity hotspots to meet their energetic requirements, and often aggregate at predictable locations. However, limited high-resolution data of the causal processes that lead to high-density concentrations of zooplankton at predator foraging grounds constitute a major obstacle to understanding their feeding environments. Certain acoustic Doppler current profilers (ADCP) have the capacity to undertake sustained (3 months) high vertical resolution (3mm) biological surveys using the integrated wideband echosounder. In this study, hydrodynamic conditions that lead to foraging events were investigated using data collected by bed-mounted, upwards-facing Nortek Signature ADCP deployed in Hanifaru Bay, the Maldives. The acoustic data were supported by in situ zooplankton samples and video surveys of M. alfredi behaviour to provide a representative baseline to validate the acoustic backscatter measurements from the ADCP. These localised datasets that link the hydrodynamic mechanisms responsible for plankton accumulation to the foraging landscape of M. alfredi will help to understand the mechanisms that link predator-prey interactions to the properties of the habitat. The novel use of this technology expands the application of ADCP data for taxa that are complex and difficult to observe.

4330: Reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) are a K-selected species characterized by low reproductive potential with long gestation times and live births to single pups at a time. Their life-history traits make them vulnerable to anthropogenic pressures, and populations are classified as vulnerable to extinction. Yet, reproductive patterns and associated habitats are still poorly understood. Here, the Project Manta photo ID database was examined to study reproductive patterns of M. alfredi on Australia's east coast. Between 2007 and 2021, 8280 sightings of 1592 individuals were recorded between Saunders Reef (11.30°S) and South West Rocks (30.9°S). 301 pregnancies among 762 females were recorded. Noticeably, some females were reported pregnant in consecutive years, although resting periods varied among individuals. Pregnancies recorded around Lady Elliot Island (LEI) and North Stradbroke Island (NSI) broadly followed temporal patterns, with pregnant individuals commonly sighted at LEI in late June before moving to NSI during Austral summer to give birth. These are preliminary results as data are currently being analysed. Moving forward, this research aims to establish a standardized framework in collaboration with the Okinawa Churaumi Aquarium. By identifying visual cues of each pregnancy stage, this study will provide recommendations to minimize observer bias and maximize the effective use of photo IDs for future databases.
